whatIs: The CSS Formatter is a client-side code beautifier that uses Prettier's PostCSS plugin to parse and reformat CSS according to standard style conventions. It automatically inserts consistent indentation, line breaks, and spacing — transforming minified or poorly formatted CSS into a readable, standardized layout. The formatter respects CSS syntax rules, preserving selectors, properties, values, and at-rules while reorganizing whitespace for maximum readability.
howToUse: Paste your CSS code into the input area on the left side of the tool.
Click the Transform button to trigger formatting. Prettier's PostCSS parser processes the input entirely in your browser — no server call is made.
The reformatted CSS appears in the output panel. Copy it with the built-in copy button or select it manually.
whyUse: Consistent CSS formatting is essential for team collaboration, code reviews, and long-term maintainability. Unformatted CSS — especially CSS generated by preprocessors, build tools, or third-party libraries — is difficult to read and debug. The CSS Formatter standardizes style across your codebase in a single action, eliminating formatting debates and making every file equally navigable.

faq.q: Does the formatter change my CSS logic?
faq.a: No. The formatter only adjusts whitespace, indentation, and line breaks. It does not modify property values, selector specificity, or any functional behavior of your CSS.

faq.q: What CSS features are supported?
faq.a: The formatter supports standard CSS including nested selectors (CSS Nesting spec), at-rules like @media and @keyframes, custom properties, and modern functions like clamp() and min(). It uses Prettier's full PostCSS plugin.

faq.q: Is there a maximum input size?
faq.a: The tool works entirely in your browser's memory. Extremely large files (over several megabytes) may slow down depending on your device, but there is no hard limit.

faq.q: Can I use this for SCSS or LESS?
faq.a: This tool uses the PostCSS parser, which handles standard CSS. For SCSS or LESS syntax, you would need a dedicated Sass/Less formatter, as those preprocessors have different parsing rules.

whatIs: The CSS Minifier strips all unnecessary characters from CSS code to produce the smallest possible file size without changing functionality. It removes comments, collapses whitespace, eliminates trailing semicolons before closing braces, and shortens hex color codes (for example, converting #ffffff to #fff). The result is production-ready CSS that loads faster due to reduced file size.
howToUse: Paste your formatted CSS into the input textarea.
Click the Transform button to minify the code. The tool runs a series of regex-based transformations entirely in your browser.
The minified output appears in the output panel with a size comparison showing the original versus compressed byte count.
whyUse: CSS minification typically reduces file size by 20 to 40 percent, which directly improves page load performance. Every kilobyte saved reduces network transfer time, especially impactful for mobile users on slower connections. Minified CSS is a standard step in production build pipelines for any web application.

faq.q: Will minification break my CSS?
faq.a: No. The minifier uses safe transformations: removing comments, collapsing whitespace, and shortening color codes. It does not merge selectors, reorder properties, or alter any CSS logic.

faq.q: How does this differ from build-tool minification?
faq.a: This tool performs the same core transformations as tools like cssnano or clean-css but runs entirely in your browser. It is useful for quick one-off minification without setting up a build pipeline.

faq.q: Does it support modern CSS features?
faq.a: Yes. The minifier handles modern syntax including CSS custom properties, calc(), clamp(), container queries, and nested selectors, since it primarily operates on whitespace and comments rather than parsing the full CSS grammar.

faq.q: What is the typical compression ratio?
faq.a: Well-formatted CSS typically compresses by 20 to 40 percent. Code that is already partially minified or very compact will see smaller reductions.

whatIs: The Box Shadow Generator is an interactive visual tool that builds CSS box-shadow declarations through real-time parameter adjustment. It controls six properties: horizontal offset (X), vertical offset (Y), blur radius, spread radius, shadow color (via a color picker), and an optional inset toggle. The tool outputs the exact CSS declaration and shows a live preview of the shadow applied to a sample element.
howToUse: Adjust the X and Y offset sliders to control the shadow's horizontal and vertical position relative to the element.
Set the Blur value to control shadow softness — higher values produce more diffused edges.
Set the Spread value to expand or contract the shadow beyond the element's boundaries.
Pick a shadow color using the color picker input.
Toggle the inset checkbox to create an inner shadow instead of an outer shadow.
Copy the generated CSS declaration from the output panel.
whyUse: Box-shadow is one of the most used CSS decorative properties, but its four numeric parameters and color value make it tedious to get right by hand. The visual generator lets you iterate on shadow appearance in real time, seeing the effect immediately rather than guessing values and refreshing a browser tab. It is particularly useful for creating depth, elevation, and focus states in UI design.

faq.q: Can I stack multiple box shadows?
faq.a: This tool generates a single box-shadow declaration. For stacked shadows, generate each shadow separately and combine them in your CSS with commas between declarations.

faq.q: Does it support RGBA or HSLA colors?
faq.a: The color picker outputs hex values. To use RGBA or HSLA, copy the shadow structure and replace the hex color with your preferred color format manually.

faq.q: What is the difference between blur and spread?
faq.a: Blur controls how soft or sharp the shadow edges are. Spread controls the shadow's size relative to the element — a positive spread makes the shadow larger, negative makes it smaller.

faq.q: Is the preview accurate to real rendering?
faq.a: The preview uses the same CSS box-shadow property that browsers render, so what you see matches actual browser output. Minor rendering differences may occur between browser engines.

whatIs: The Text Shadow Generator creates CSS text-shadow declarations through interactive controls. It adjusts four properties: horizontal offset, vertical offset, blur radius, and shadow color. The tool renders a live preview showing the shadow applied to sample text, and outputs the complete CSS property ready for use in stylesheets.
howToUse: Set the X and Y offset values to control where the shadow falls relative to the text.
Adjust the Blur radius — a value of 0 produces a sharp shadow, while higher values create a soft glow effect.
Choose a shadow color using the color picker.
Copy the generated text-shadow CSS from the output panel.
whyUse: Text-shadow adds depth, readability, and visual hierarchy to headings, hero sections, and call-to-action text. The blur and color controls make it straightforward to create effects ranging from subtle lift to dramatic neon glows, all without writing CSS by trial and error.

faq.q: Can I create multiple text shadows?
faq.a: Generate one shadow at a time. For layered effects, combine multiple text-shadow values separated by commas in your CSS, each with different offsets or colors.

faq.q: Does text-shadow affect text readability?
faq.a: Poorly chosen shadow colors or excessive blur can reduce readability. Generally, use a darker or lighter shade of the text color with a small offset for legibility-enhancing shadows.

faq.q: Does this work with web fonts?
faq.a: Yes. The text-shadow property applies to any rendered text regardless of font family. The preview uses a system font, but the generated CSS works identically with custom web fonts.

whatIs: The Border Radius Generator creates CSS border-radius values for all four corners — top-left, top-right, bottom-right, and bottom-left. Each corner accepts an independent pixel value, allowing asymmetric rounding. The tool shows a live preview of the resulting shape on a gradient-filled element, and outputs the exact CSS declaration.
howToUse: Enter a pixel value for each corner: TL (top-left), TR (top-right), BR (bottom-right), and BL (bottom-left).
The preview updates in real time, showing how the combined radii shape the element.
Copy the generated border-radius declaration from the output panel.
whyUse: The border-radius shorthand property requires four values in clockwise order, which is easy to get wrong. This tool lets you visually configure each corner independently, making it simple to create pill shapes, organic blobs, notched cards, and other common UI patterns without mental gymnastics about value ordering.

faq.q: Can I create a perfect circle?
faq.a: Yes. Set all four corners to at least 50 percent of the element's width and height. A square element with 50px on all corners becomes a circle.

faq.q: What is the shorthand syntax?
faq.a: The output uses the four-value shorthand: top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left. This matches the clockwise reading order specified in the CSS specification.

faq.q: Does border-radius clip content?
faq.a: By default, content (including backgrounds and images) is clipped to the rounded corners. To prevent clipping, add overflow: hidden to the element.

whatIs: The CSS Triangle Generator creates pure CSS triangles using the border-width technique. It generates the border and border-color properties needed to render a triangle pointing in any of four directions (up, down, left, right) at a configurable size and color. The output includes the width, height, and border declarations required, with a live preview of the resulting shape.
howToUse: Select the triangle direction from the dropdown: Up, Down, Left, or Right.
Set the Size value in pixels — this controls the triangle's leg length.
Pick a color using the color picker.
Copy the generated CSS from the output panel and apply it to a div with width: 0 and height: 0.
whyUse: CSS triangles are a common UI element for tooltips, dropdown menus, chat bubbles, and directional indicators. The border-based technique is tricky because it relies on transparent borders adjacent to a colored border on one side. This tool eliminates the mental calculation by generating the exact values needed.

faq.q: Why is width: 0 and height: 0 required?
faq.a: The triangle technique works by making the element zero-sized so only the borders are visible. The colored border forms the triangle while the transparent borders create the cut-away shape.

faq.q: Can I make right-angle triangles?
faq.a: The standard output creates isosceles triangles. For right-angle triangles, you can adjust the border widths asymmetrically — set different values for the two adjacent border sides.

faq.q: Does this work in all browsers?
faq.a: Yes. The CSS border triangle technique is supported in all modern browsers and has been stable since Internet Explorer 6. It relies on fundamental CSS box model behavior.

whatIs: The CSS Filter Generator creates a combined CSS filter declaration using six adjustable parameters: blur (in pixels), brightness, contrast, grayscale, sepia, and hue-rotate (in degrees). It renders a live preview on a gradient-filled sample element so you can see the visual effect of each adjustment in real time, and outputs the complete filter property value.
howToUse: Adjust the Blur slider to add Gaussian blur to the element.
Set Brightness to control overall luminance — values above 100 lighten, below 100 darken.
Set Contrast to increase or decrease the difference between light and dark areas.
Set Grayscale to desaturate the element — 100% produces full grayscale.
Set Sepia to add a warm brownish tone — 100% produces full sepia.
Set Hue to rotate the hue angle, shifting all colors around the color wheel.
Copy the generated filter declaration from the output panel.
whyUse: The CSS filter property accepts a chain of filter functions, and combining multiple effects while keeping values balanced requires careful tuning. The visual preview lets you see how blur, brightness, contrast, and color shifts interact when stacked together, producing a polished filter chain without repeatedly refreshing a browser.

faq.q: Do filters affect layout or just rendering?
faq.a: CSS filters only affect visual rendering. They do not change the element's layout, dimensions, or position in the document flow.

faq.q: Are filters performant?
faq.a: Blur and complex filter chains can be expensive for large elements. Consider applying filters to small elements or using will-change: filter for GPU-accelerated rendering.

faq.q: Can I animate CSS filters?
faq.a: Yes. All filter functions are animatable. Transition or animate the filter property to smoothly shift between different filter states.

faq.q: Does filter affect child elements?
faq.a: Yes. A filter applied to a parent element affects the visual rendering of all its children. The entire subtree is filtered as a composite image.

whatIs: The Cubic Bezier Generator creates CSS cubic-bezier timing function values by letting you visually configure the two control points of a cubic Bézier curve. It outputs the cubic-bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2) function used in CSS transitions and animations, and shows a live animation of an element moving according to the generated timing curve so you can see the acceleration and deceleration behavior.
howToUse: Adjust the four control point values: X1, Y1, X2, and Y2. X1 and X2 must be between 0 and 1; Y1 and Y2 can extend beyond that range for overshoot effects.
Watch the animated preview block move back and forth, demonstrating the timing curve's easing behavior.
Copy the generated transition or animation CSS from the output panel.
whyUse: CSS transitions default to ease timing, but custom cubic-bezier curves give precise control over animation feel — from snappy pop-in effects to smooth elastic bounces. The standard easing presets (ease, ease-in, ease-out, ease-in-out) are all cubic-bezier values, and this tool lets you create custom curves beyond those presets with immediate visual feedback.

faq.q: What are the common easing presets?
faq.a: ease is cubic-bezier(0.25, 0.1, 0.25, 1), ease-in is cubic-bezier(0.42, 0, 1, 1), ease-out is cubic-bezier(0, 0, 0.58, 1), and ease-in-out is cubic-bezier(0.42, 0, 0.58, 1).

faq.q: What does Y > 1 or Y < 0 do?
faq.a: Y values outside the 0 to 1 range create overshoot effects. Values above 1 cause the animation to temporarily exceed the target, while values below 0 cause it to start from below the starting point.

faq.q: Is this the same as CSS spring animations?
faq.a: No. CSS spring animations are a separate spec not yet widely supported. Cubic-bezier provides an approximation but cannot truly model spring physics with oscillation.

whatIs: The CSS Unit Converter converts between CSS measurement units: pixels (px), rem, em, and points (pt). Enter one or more numeric values and it outputs the equivalent in all four unit formats simultaneously. The converter accepts a configurable base font size (default 16px) for accurate rem and em calculations.
howToUse: Select the source unit from the dropdown: px, rem, em, or pt.
Set the base font size in pixels if your project uses a non-default root font size.
Enter one or more numeric values separated by spaces or commas.
Click Transform to see each value converted to all four unit formats.
whyUse: Modern CSS uses a mix of units — rem for scalable spacing, px for precise borders, pt for print media, and em for component-relative sizing. Converting between them manually is tedious and error-prone, especially when working with design systems that specify values in px while your codebase uses rem. This tool handles the math instantly.

faq.q: What is the default base font size?
faq.a: The default is 16px, matching the browser's default root font size. Most projects should keep this default unless their root font-size is explicitly set to a different value.

faq.q: What is the difference between rem and em?
faq.a: rem is always relative to the root (html) font size. em is relative to the current element's font size. In practice, rem provides more predictable, consistent spacing across components.

faq.q: Why use points (pt)?
faq.a: Points are primarily used in print CSS. One point equals 1/72 of an inch. For screen display, px, rem, or em are generally preferred.

whatIs: The Rem PX Converter is a dedicated bidirectional converter between rem and pixel units. It supports two conversion directions — px to rem and rem to px — with a configurable base font size (default 16px). Enter one or more values and get the converted results immediately.
howToUse: Select the conversion direction: px to rem or rem to px.
Set the base font size in pixels if your project uses a non-default root size.
Enter numeric values separated by spaces or commas.
Click Transform to see the converted values.
whyUse: Converting between rem and px is the most frequent unit conversion in modern web development. Design systems and style guides often specify spacing in px while CSS codebases prefer rem for scalability. This tool provides a focused, single-purpose converter without the overhead of a full unit converter.

faq.q: Why prefer rem over px?
faq.a: Rem scales with the root font size, making layouts responsive to user zoom preferences and accessibility settings. Px values are fixed and do not adapt.

faq.q: What if my root font size is 14px?
faq.a: Change the base value to 14. The converter will use 14px as the reference for all rem calculations.

faq.q: Can I convert fractional rem values?
faq.a: Yes. The converter handles decimal values like 1.25rem or 0.75rem and outputs precise pixel equivalents.

whatIs: The Clamp Calculator generates CSS clamp() expressions for fluid typography and spacing. It takes a minimum value, maximum value, minimum viewport width, and maximum viewport width, then computes the preferred value using linear interpolation between the breakpoints. The output is a ready-to-use clamp() declaration that smoothly scales between the min and max across the specified viewport range.
howToUse: Enter the minimum value in pixels (the size at the smallest viewport).
Enter the maximum value in pixels (the size at the largest viewport).
Enter the minimum viewport width in pixels (e.g., 400 for mobile).
Enter the maximum viewport width in pixels (e.g., 1200 for desktop).
The tool outputs the clamp() expression with the calculated preferred value.
whyUse: The CSS clamp() function replaces complex media query chains for responsive typography and spacing, but calculating the preferred value requires slope and intercept math. This tool automates that calculation, producing a single clamp() declaration that works across all viewport sizes between your breakpoints.

faq.q: What does the output clamp() expression mean?
faq.a: clamp(min, preferred, max) ensures the value never goes below min, never above max, and scales linearly via the preferred expression across the viewport range.

faq.q: Can I use this for font-size?
faq.a: Yes. Set min to your base font size, max to your heading size, and the viewport widths to your design breakpoints. The output scales smoothly between those sizes.

faq.q: What viewport widths should I use?
faq.a: Common ranges are 320 to 1280 for mobile-first designs, or 400 to 1440 for broader ranges. Match your project's actual design breakpoints.

whatIs: The CSS Specificity Calculator parses a CSS selector and computes its specificity score using the standard (IDs, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, elements) notation. Enter any CSS selector — including complex compound selectors with combinators, attribute selectors, and pseudo-classes — and the tool counts each category to determine which selector wins in a specificity tie.
howToUse: Type or paste a CSS selector into the input field (e.g., div.container > .item[data-active]::before).
Click Transform to calculate specificity.
The output shows the ID count, class/attribute/pseudo-class count, element count, and the decimal specificity value.
whyUse: Understanding CSS specificity is critical for debugging style conflicts, especially in large codebases or when working with CSS frameworks. The (IDs, classes, elements) notation is simple in theory but difficult to apply manually on complex selectors with multiple pseudo-classes, attribute selectors, and combinators. This tool provides instant, reliable specificity calculations.

faq.q: What is the specificity weight of each category?
faq.a: IDs count as 100 each, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes count as 10 each, and elements/pseudo-elements count as 1 each. A selector with 2 IDs and 3 classes scores (2, 3, 0) = 230.

faq.q: How are pseudo-elements counted?
faq.a: Pseudo-elements like ::before and ::after are counted in the element category, not the class category. This matches the CSS specification's specificity rules.

faq.q: Does :not() affect specificity?
faq.a: The :not() pseudo-class itself has zero specificity, but the selector inside it contributes its own specificity to the overall score.

faq.q: What about inline styles?
faq.a: Inline styles (style attributes) have a specificity of (1, 0, 0, 0) — higher than any selector-based specificity. This tool calculates selector specificity only.

whatIs: The Tailwind Class Sorter organizes Tailwind CSS utility classes into a consistent, predictable order. It sorts classes by category — layout (flex, grid, block), sizing (w, h), spacing (p, m), typography (text, font), visual (bg, border, rounded, shadow) — and alphabetically within each category. The output is the same classes in a standardized sequence that matches Tailwind's recommended ordering.
howToUse: Paste a space-separated list of Tailwind CSS utility classes into the input area.
Click Transform to sort the classes.
Copy the sorted output. The classes are reordered but identical in content — no classes are added or removed.
whyUse: Tailwind class ordering is a common source of code review friction. Developers naturally write classes in different orders, creating noisy diffs and inconsistent style across a team. Sorting classes to a standard order eliminates this noise, makes diffs cleaner, and ensures every file follows the same convention.

faq.q: Does sorting change how the CSS renders?
faq.a: No. The order of classes in an HTML class attribute does not affect CSS specificity or rendering. Sorting is purely a code organization convention.

faq.q: What sorting order is used?
faq.a: Classes are grouped by category (layout, sizing, spacing, typography, visual) following the order Tailwind's official documentation presents utilities. Within each group, classes are sorted alphabetically.

faq.q: Does this work with Tailwind v4?
faq.a: The sorting logic is based on class name prefixes, which are consistent across Tailwind versions. It works with v3 and v4 utility classes.

whatIs: The Tailwind Class Merger combines two sets of Tailwind CSS utility classes into a single, deduplicated list. When both sets contain classes with the same prefix (e.g., two different padding values), the second set wins, matching Tailwind's cascade behavior. The output is a single space-separated string of classes with all conflicts resolved.
howToUse: Paste the first set of Tailwind classes in the left input area.
Paste the second set of Tailwind classes in the right input area (or second input).
Click Transform to merge the sets.
The output shows the merged class list with a count of how many classes were combined and deduplicated.
whyUse: When building component libraries or composing utility classes from different sources (base styles, variant overrides, conditional classes), you often end up with duplicate class prefixes. Tailwind resolves conflicts by applying the last class in source order, but manually deduplicating is tedious. This tool automates the merge, keeping only the final value for each utility prefix.

faq.q: How are conflicts resolved?
faq.a: When two classes share the same prefix (e.g., p-4 and p-8), the class from the second set wins. This matches Tailwind's behavior where later classes in source order override earlier ones.

faq.q: What counts as a prefix?
faq.a: The prefix is the part of the class name before any digit or bracket. For example, p-4 and p-[20px] share the prefix p-. bg-red-500 and bg-blue-300 share the prefix bg-.

faq.q: Does this handle responsive and state variants?
faq.a: Yes. Responsive prefixes (sm:, md:, lg:) and state prefixes (hover:, focus:) are preserved. Classes like hover:bg-red-500 and hover:bg-blue-500 share the same hover: prefix and are treated as a conflict.

whatIs: The CSS to Tailwind Converter maps individual CSS declarations to their Tailwind CSS utility class equivalents. Paste CSS properties and the tool attempts to find a matching Tailwind class for each declaration. For declarations with no direct Tailwind equivalent, it notes that no common class exists. The output shows each CSS line alongside its Tailwind equivalent or a fallback note.
howToUse: Paste CSS declarations into the input area — individual property-value pairs, not full rule blocks.
Click Transform to see the mapping.
Each line shows the original CSS declaration, an arrow, and the matching Tailwind class or a note that no equivalent exists.
whyUse: Migrating from vanilla CSS to Tailwind requires mapping existing property-value pairs to utility classes. This mapping is straightforward for common properties (display: flex becomes flex) but less obvious for others. The converter provides instant lookup, accelerating the migration process and serving as a learning tool for Tailwind newcomers.

faq.q: Does this support all Tailwind utilities?
faq.a: The converter covers the most common CSS-to-Tailwind mappings: display, flexbox, spacing, typography, borders, colors, and alignment. Rare or complex declarations may not have direct equivalents.

faq.q: What about arbitrary values?
faq.a: Tailwind v3+ supports arbitrary values like p-[20px] for CSS properties without preset utilities. This tool maps to standard utility classes, not arbitrary value syntax.

faq.q: Can I paste entire CSS rule blocks?
faq.a: The tool works best with individual declarations. It strips braces and semicolons automatically, but the output is more accurate when you paste clean property-value pairs.

whatIs: The SVG Blob Generator creates organic, irregular blob shapes using cubic Bézier curves in SVG path format. It generates a random blob each time you click the transform button, producing unique SVG output with smooth, curved edges. The blob is defined by a series of control points that create natural-looking, asymmetric shapes suitable for decorative backgrounds, profile images, or UI accents.
howToUse: Click the Transform button to generate a new random blob shape.
Each click produces a different blob with a random number of control points (6 to 10) and varied radii.
Copy the SVG output from the output panel. The SVG uses currentColor for fill, making it inherit the text color of its parent element.
whyUse: Organic blob shapes are a popular design trend used for hero section backgrounds, profile image masks, decorative elements, and call-to-action highlights. Hand-coding smooth Bézier curves for irregular shapes is mathematically complex. This generator produces ready-to-use SVG blobs with natural curvature that would be difficult to design manually.

faq.q: Can I control the blob shape?
faq.a: Each generation is random. Click multiple times until you get a shape you like. The generator produces 6 to 10 control points with randomized radii for variety.

faq.q: How do I change the blob color?
faq.a: The SVG uses currentColor as the fill value, so the blob inherits the text color of its parent CSS context. Set color on the parent element or replace currentColor with a specific color value.

faq.q: Can I animate the blob?
faq.a: Yes. You can animate the SVG path using CSS or SMIL animations, or transition between different blob shapes using SVG path morphing libraries.

whatIs: The SVG Wave Generator creates layered wave patterns using SVG path elements with sinusoidal curves. It produces multiple overlapping wave layers with decreasing opacity, creating a depth effect commonly used in hero sections and page footers. The output is a complete SVG element with the wave pattern ready to embed in any web page.
howToUse: Click the Transform button to generate a new wave pattern.
The generator creates three layered wave paths with varying amplitude, frequency, and opacity.
Copy the SVG output and embed it in your HTML. The waves use rgba colors for the layered depth effect.
whyUse: Wave separators between page sections are a widely used design pattern, but hand-coding sinusoidal SVG paths with correct control points is mathematically tedious. This generator produces production-ready wave SVGs with natural-looking curves and layered depth, saving significant time on hero sections and section dividers.

faq.q: Can I customize the wave colors?
faq.a: The generated SVG uses hardcoded rgba values. To change colors, replace the rgba fill values in the output with your preferred colors.

faq.q: How many layers are generated?
faq.a: The generator creates three wave layers with progressively lower opacity, creating a natural depth-of-field effect.

faq.q: Can I use this as a CSS background?
faq.a: Yes. Encode the SVG as a data URI and use it with background-image, or embed the SVG directly in your HTML for easier styling.

whatIs: The SVG Background Generator creates tileable SVG patterns for use as CSS backgrounds. Each generation produces one of several pattern types — polka dots, diagonal lines, or concentric circles — using subtle, low-contrast colors suitable for page backgrounds. The output includes both the raw SVG and a CSS background-image data URI for immediate use.
howToUse: Click the Transform button to generate a new random pattern.
The tool outputs the SVG source code and renders a preview showing how the tiled pattern looks at 200px height.
Copy either the SVG source or use the preview to verify the pattern before applying it to your project.
whyUse: Subtle background patterns add visual texture to web pages without the weight of raster images. SVG patterns are resolution-independent, tiny in file size, and can be embedded directly as data URIs. This generator produces ready-to-use tileable patterns without requiring knowledge of SVG pattern elements or coordinate math.

faq.q: Are these patterns tileable?
faq.a: Yes. All generated patterns are designed to tile seamlessly both horizontally and vertically when used as CSS backgrounds.

faq.q: How do I apply this as a CSS background?
faq.a: Encode the SVG as a data URI: background-image: url('data:image/svg+xml,<encoded SVG>');. The pattern tiles automatically.

faq.q: Can I change the pattern colors?
faq.a: The patterns use fixed pastel colors for subtlety. To customize, edit the fill and stroke values in the SVG output.

whatIs: The SVG to JSX Converter transforms standard SVG markup into valid React JSX syntax. It automatically converts HTML SVG attributes to their JSX equivalents: class becomes className, fill-rule becomes fillRule, clip-path becomes clipPath, and xlink references are handled correctly. The output includes a React functional component wrapper for immediate use in React projects.
howToUse: Paste your standard SVG markup into the input area.
Click Transform to convert the SVG to JSX.
The output includes the converted JSX wrapped in a React component with spread props support.
whyUse: SVG elements use HTML attribute names (class, fill-rule, clip-path) that conflict with React's JSX syntax requirements. Manually renaming every attribute is tedious and error-prone, especially for complex SVGs with many attributes. This converter handles the full mapping automatically, producing copy-paste-ready React components.

faq.q: What attributes are converted?
faq.a: class becomes className, fill-rule becomes fillRule, clip-path becomes clipPath, clip-rule becomes clipRule, and xlink: attributes are converted to xlinkHref. All other attributes pass through unchanged.

faq.q: Does this support React Native?
faq.a: The output uses standard React SVG components. For React Native, you would need to use react-native-svg with its own component names (Svg, Path, Circle, etc.), which this tool does not currently handle.

faq.q: Can I add props to the generated component?
faq.a: Yes. The component includes { ...props } spread, so you can pass className, style, onClick, and any other standard React props to the wrapper.

whatIs: The SVG Path Editor parses SVG path data strings and breaks them down into individual commands with their coordinates. It identifies each command type (Move, Line, Cubic Bezier, Quadratic Bezier, Arc, Close) and displays them as an indexed list, making it easy to understand the structure of complex SVG paths without reading dense coordinate strings.
howToUse: Paste SVG path data into the input field (the d attribute value from an SVG path element).
Click Transform to parse the path.
The output shows each command indexed and labeled, with the command letter and its coordinate parameters.
whyUse: SVG path data is notoriously difficult to read — a complex shape might be a single string of hundreds of coordinates with no separators. Understanding which commands are Move (M), Line (L), Cubic Bezier (C), or Arc (A) is essential for debugging rendering issues, modifying shapes, or converting between SVG editors. This tool makes path data human-readable.

faq.q: What SVG path commands are supported?
faq.a: All standard SVG path commands are parsed: M/m (move), L/l (line), H/h (horizontal line), V/v (vertical line), C/c (cubic Bezier), S/s (smooth cubic), Q/q (quadratic), T/t (smooth quadratic), A/a (arc), and Z/z (close path).

faq.q: Does this edit the path visually?
faq.a: No. This is a text-based parser that displays path structure. For visual path editing, you would need a dedicated SVG editor.

faq.q: Can I paste full SVG markup?
faq.a: The tool expects just the path data (the d attribute value), not the full <path> element. Extract the d attribute content before pasting.

whatIs: The SVG Filter Generator creates SVG filter definitions using standard SVG filter primitives. It produces a complete set of filter definitions including blur (feGaussianBlur), grayscale (feColorMatrix saturate), sepia (feColorMatrix matrix), invert (feColorMatrix), and contrast (feComponentTransfer). The output includes the full SVG defs block ready to embed, with filter IDs for use via CSS filter: url(#id).
howToUse: Click the Transform button to generate a complete set of SVG filter definitions.
The output includes five filter definitions with unique IDs: blur, gray, sepia, invert, and contrast.
Embed the defs block in your SVG or reference the filters via CSS using filter: url(#blur) syntax.
whyUse: SVG filters provide capabilities beyond CSS filters, including custom convolution matrices, lighting effects, and compositing operations. However, the SVG filter syntax with feGaussianBlur, feColorMatrix, and feComponentTransfer is verbose and difficult to write by hand. This generator produces correct, complete filter definitions for common visual effects.

faq.q: How do I apply these filters?
faq.a: Reference them via CSS: filter: url(#blur);. Or apply directly in SVG using filter="url(#blur)" on any element.

faq.q: Can I combine multiple filters?
faq.a: Yes. Use CSS filter chaining: filter: url(#blur) url(#sepia);. Or create a custom SVG filter that chains filter primitives within a single filter element.

faq.q: Do SVG filters work in all browsers?
faq.a: SVG filters are well-supported in all modern browsers. Internet Explorer had limited support, but it is no longer relevant for modern web development.

whatIs: The SVG Clip Path Generator creates SVG clipPath definitions for masking content to specific shapes. It generates three shape options — circle, triangle, and star — as clipPath elements that can be applied to any SVG or HTML element. The output includes the complete SVG defs block with the clipPath and a preview showing a rectangle clipped to the generated shape.
howToUse: Click the Transform button to generate a random clip shape (circle, triangle, or star).
The output includes the SVG clipPath definition and a preview showing a filled rectangle clipped to the shape.
Apply the clip-path to any element via CSS: clip-path: url(#circle-clip); or directly in SVG attributes.
whyUse: SVG clip paths let you mask elements to arbitrary shapes — circles, polygons, stars, or any custom path. This is useful for profile images, decorative framing, creative section masking, and any visual design that goes beyond rectangular containers. The generator produces correct clipPath definitions without requiring knowledge of SVG coordinate systems.

faq.q: Can I use these with HTML elements?
faq.a: Yes. Apply via CSS: clip-path: url(#circle-clip);. Make sure the clipPath SVG is included in your page or referenced via an external SVG file.

faq.q: How do I change the clipped element's content?
faq.a: Replace the placeholder rect with whatever content you want to clip — an image, text, or any other SVG elements.

faq.q: Can I create custom shapes?
faq.a: The generator produces predefined shapes. For custom shapes, modify the polygon points or circle/triangle coordinates in the output SVG.

whatIs: The CSS Flexbox Visual Builder is an interactive playground that demonstrates CSS Flexbox layout properties in real time. It renders five numbered items inside a flex container and provides controls for justify-content, align-items, flex-direction, and flex-wrap. Changes update instantly, and the corresponding CSS declarations are displayed below the preview for copying.
howToUse: Use the dropdown controls to change justify-content, align-items, flex-direction, and flex-wrap values.
Watch the five numbered boxes rearrange in real time as you adjust each property.
Copy the generated CSS from the code block below the preview.
whyUse: Flexbox is the most common CSS layout system, but understanding how justify-content and align-items interact with different flex-direction values requires visual experimentation. This playground eliminates the need to switch between code editor and browser tab, letting you see the effect of every property combination instantly.

faq.q: What flexbox properties can I adjust?
faq.a: Four properties: justify-content (main axis alignment), align-items (cross axis alignment), flex-direction (axis orientation), and flex-wrap (wrapping behavior).

faq.q: Can I change the number of items?
faq.a: The playground renders five fixed items. The CSS output works with any number of flex children in your actual project.

faq.q: Is the generated CSS complete?
faq.a: The output includes display: flex and the four selected properties. You may need to add gap, padding, or other properties for your specific use case.

whatIs: The CSS Grid Visual Builder is an interactive playground for CSS Grid layout. It renders a configurable grid with adjustable columns, rows, and gap values. Numbered grid items fill the cells automatically, and the corresponding CSS grid declarations are displayed below the preview for direct use in your stylesheets.
howToUse: Set the number of columns using the Cols input (1 to 8).
Set the number of rows using the Rows input (1 to 6).
Adjust the Gap value in pixels to control spacing between grid cells.
Copy the generated CSS from the code block below the grid preview.
whyUse: CSS Grid is powerful but abstract — understanding how repeat(), grid-template-columns, and gap interact requires experimentation. The visual builder shows exactly how column and row counts create cell layouts, with immediate CSS output for the configuration you see.

faq.q: Does this support fr units?
faq.a: The generator uses repeat(N, 1fr) for equal-width columns. For custom column widths, modify the output CSS to use different track sizes.

faq.q: Can I create spanning items?
faq.a: The playground renders simple grid items that each occupy one cell. For grid-column or grid-row spanning, modify the generated CSS with additional grid item properties.

faq.q: What is the maximum grid size?
faq.a: Columns go up to 8 and rows up to 6, for a maximum of 48 cells. This covers most common grid layouts.

whatIs: The CSS Animation Generator produces ready-to-use CSS keyframe animations with matching animation properties. It includes four preset animations — bounce, fade-in, spin, and pulse — each with their @keyframes definition and shorthand animation declaration. Click Transform to get a random animation, or use the output as a starting point for customization.
howToUse: Click the Transform button to generate a random animation preset.
The output includes both the @keyframes rule and the .animated class with the animation shorthand.
Copy both the keyframes and class definitions into your stylesheet.
whyUse: Writing CSS animations from scratch requires coordinating @keyframes definitions with animation shorthand properties — duration, timing-function, iteration-count, and direction. The generator provides four common animation patterns as starting points, complete with correct keyframe percentages and timing values.

faq.q: What animations are included?
faq.a: Four presets: bounce (vertical oscillation), fade-in (opacity and translateY), spin (360-degree rotation), and pulse (scale oscillation).

faq.q: How do I customize the duration?
faq.a: Change the duration value in the animation shorthand property. For example, change animation: bounce 0.6s infinite to animation: bounce 1.2s infinite for a slower bounce.

faq.q: Can I apply this to any element?
faq.a: Yes. Add the generated class name to any HTML element. The animation starts immediately by default — add animation-delay for staggered effects.

whatIs: The CSS Loader Generator creates pure CSS loading indicators — animated spinners, bouncing dots, and sliding bars — that require no images, SVGs, or JavaScript. Each loader is defined entirely in CSS using keyframe animations, border-radius tricks, and pseudo-elements. The output includes the complete CSS for one randomly selected loader type.
howToUse: Click the Transform button to generate a random loader type.
Three loader types are available: Spinner (rotating border), Dots (bouncing circles), and Bar (sliding progress bar).
Copy the generated CSS and add the corresponding HTML structure to your page.
whyUse: Loading indicators are needed on nearly every web application, but most implementations rely on GIFs, SVGs, or JavaScript animation libraries. Pure CSS loaders are zero-dependency, resolution-independent, and trivially customizable. The generator provides production-ready patterns for the three most common loader styles.

faq.q: What HTML structure do these loaders need?
faq.a: The spinner uses a single div, dots use three span elements inside a container div, and the bar uses a single div. Each loader's HTML is minimal.

faq.q: Can I change the loader color?
faq.a: Replace the #4f46e5 primary color in the CSS with any color value. The #e5e7eb track color can also be customized.

faq.q: Do these work in all browsers?
faq.a: Yes. CSS animations and border-radius are universally supported. These loaders work in all modern browsers and IE11+.

whatIs: The CSS Clip Path Generator creates CSS clip-path declarations for non-rectangular element shapes. It generates random clip-path values including circle, polygon, hexagon, and cross shapes. The output includes both the CSS property and a live preview showing a gradient-filled element clipped to the generated shape.
howToUse: Click the Transform button to generate a new random clip-path shape.
The preview shows a gradient-filled element clipped to the generated shape.
Copy the clip-path CSS declaration from the output panel.
whyUse: CSS clip-path enables creative layouts — circles for profile images, hexagons for feature cards, custom polygons for unique section shapes. However, calculating polygon coordinates or circle percentages by hand is tedious. This generator produces correct clip-path values with immediate visual feedback.

faq.q: What shapes can be generated?
faq.a: The generator produces circle(), polygon() (diamond, hexagon, cross), and ellipse() clip-path values with random parameters.

faq.q: Does clip-path affect layout?
faq.a: No. clip-path only affects visual rendering. The element retains its original layout dimensions and spacing.

faq.q: Can I animate clip-path?
faq.a: Yes. Clip-path polygon animations are supported in modern browsers. You can transition between different polygon shapes for creative effects.

whatIs: The CSS Masking Generator creates CSS mask-image declarations using gradient-based masks. It generates three mask types — linear gradient with a hard edge, radial gradient with a soft falloff, and a vertical fade — each producing different visibility patterns. The output includes both standard and webkit-prefixed mask-image properties.
howToUse: Click the Transform button to generate a random mask type.
The output includes the mask-image declaration with both standard and -webkit-mask-image prefixed versions.
Apply the mask to any element to reveal or hide portions based on the gradient pattern.
whyUse: CSS masks use gradient patterns to control element visibility, enabling effects like text-reveal animations, image fade edges, and partial visibility transitions. The mask-image syntax is similar to background-image gradients but requires separate webkit prefixes for cross-browser compatibility, which this generator handles automatically.

faq.q: What is the difference between mask and clip-path?
faq.a: Clip-path creates hard-edged boundaries (fully visible or fully hidden). Masks use gradients to create smooth transparency transitions from fully visible to fully transparent.

faq.q: Do I need the webkit prefix?
faq.a: Currently, most browsers require the -webkit-mask-image prefix for mask support. The generator outputs both the standard and prefixed versions.

faq.q: Can masks be animated?
faq.a: Yes. Transitioning the mask-image or animating gradient positions creates reveal and conceal effects. Use transition: mask-image for smooth transitions.

whatIs: The CSS Counter Style Generator creates custom @counter-style rules for list numbering. It produces a cyclic counter using emoji symbols (colored circles) as list markers, along with the corresponding list-style assignment. The @counter-style at-rule allows defining completely custom numbering systems beyond the default decimal, disc, and circle styles.
howToUse: Click the Transform button to generate the @counter-style definition and list-style assignment.
Copy the generated CSS into your stylesheet.
Apply the list-style: emojis class to any ordered or unordered list.
whyUse: The CSS @counter-style specification enables custom list markers — emoji, icons, or any Unicode characters — without replacing list items with divs or spans. This generator provides a working example of the syntax with emoji symbols, demonstrating the system, symbols, and suffix properties.

faq.q: What is the @counter-style support?
faq.a: The @counter-style at-rule is supported in Chrome 91+, Edge 91+, and Firefox 33+. Safari does not currently support it.

faq.q: Can I use different symbols?
faq.a: Replace the emoji symbols in the symbols array with any Unicode characters, strings, or even images (using url() inside symbols).

faq.q: How does cyclic system work?
faq.a: The cyclic system repeats the symbol list. If there are 6 symbols and 10 list items, items 7 through 10 cycle back to the first 4 symbols.

whatIs: The CSS Custom Properties Inspector extracts and lists all CSS custom properties (variables) defined in a block of CSS. Paste any CSS code and the tool identifies every --variable-name: value declaration, displaying them as a clean list. This is useful for auditing design tokens, reviewing component styles, or finding variable definitions in unfamiliar codebases.
howToUse: Paste CSS code containing custom property definitions into the input area.
Click Transform to extract all custom properties.
The output lists each --property: value pair with a count of total custom properties found.
whyUse: As CSS codebases grow, custom properties accumulate across files and components. Finding all defined variables, checking their values, and understanding the token naming conventions requires reading through potentially thousands of lines. The inspector extracts this information instantly, providing a clear inventory of your CSS custom properties.

faq.q: Does it find computed values?
faq.a: No. The tool extracts custom property declarations from CSS source text. It finds --var: value patterns in the input, not runtime computed values.

faq.q: Does it detect var() usage?
faq.a: No. This inspector focuses on custom property definitions (--property: value), not var() references. It audits what is defined, not what is used.

faq.q: Can it extract variables from SCSS or LESS?
faq.a: If the SCSS or LESS output contains standard CSS custom properties, they will be extracted. However, SCSS variables ($var) and LESS variables (@var) use different syntax and are not detected.

whatIs: The CSS Transform Playground is an interactive tool for experimenting with CSS transform functions. It provides four sliders — rotate (in degrees), scale, translateX, and translateY — applied to a gradient-colored element in real time. The corresponding CSS transform declaration is displayed below the preview, showing exactly how the numeric values translate to CSS syntax.
howToUse: Adjust the Rotate slider to rotate the element from -180 to 180 degrees.
Adjust the Scale slider to scale the element from 0.5x to 2x its original size.
Adjust the X and Y sliders to translate the element horizontally and vertically.
Copy the generated transform declaration from the code block below the preview.
whyUse: CSS transforms combine multiple functions — rotate, scale, translate — into a single property, but the interaction between these functions is not intuitive. Seeing a live element respond to each slider makes it clear how transforms compose, especially the order-dependent nature of rotate-then-translate versus translate-then-rotate.

faq.q: Can I combine multiple transform functions?
faq.a: Yes. The playground applies rotate, scale, and translate simultaneously in the order: rotate first, then scale, then translate. This matches common CSS transform ordering.

faq.q: Does transform affect layout?
faq.a: No. CSS transforms are visual-only. The element retains its original position in the document flow and takes up its original space.

faq.q: How do I change the transform origin?
faq.a: Add transform-origin: center; (or any other origin point) to your CSS. The playground uses the default center origin.

whatIs: The CSS Variables Generator converts key-value pairs into a CSS :root block containing custom property declarations. Enter variables as key=value pairs, one per line, and the tool outputs a properly formatted :root { --key: value; } block ready for use in your stylesheet.
howToUse: Enter variable definitions as key=value pairs, one per line (e.g., primary=#4f46e5).
Click Transform to generate the :root CSS block.
Copy the output into your stylesheet's :root selector.
whyUse: Setting up a CSS custom property design system requires defining dozens of variables in :root syntax. Manually writing --key: value; for each token is tedious and error-prone. The generator converts a simple, readable input format into correct CSS custom property syntax.

faq.q: What naming convention should I use?
faq.a: Use descriptive, hyphenated names like primary-color, spacing-lg, or font-size-base. The generator automatically prefixes each key with --.

faq.q: Can I include units in values?
faq.a: Yes. Enter values like spacing-lg=16px or font-size-base=1rem. The unit is included as-is in the generated CSS.

faq.q: Can I define nested scopes?
faq.a: The generator creates :root-level variables. For scoped variables, modify the output to target specific selectors instead of :root.

whatIs: The Scrollbar Generator creates custom scrollbar CSS for both WebKit browsers (Chrome, Edge, Safari) and Firefox. It outputs a complete stylesheet including scrollbar width, track background, thumb color, and hover state styling. The generated CSS covers both the -webkit-scrollbar pseudo-elements and the Firefox scrollbar-width/scrollbar-color properties.
howToUse: Click the Transform button to generate the scrollbar CSS.
The output includes WebKit scrollbar styles (-webkit-scrollbar, -webkit-scrollbar-track, -webkit-scrollbar-thumb) and Firefox scrollbar properties.
Copy the entire CSS block into your stylesheet. Customize the colors and widths to match your design.
whyUse: Custom scrollbars improve visual consistency in web applications, but the CSS syntax differs between WebKit and Firefox browsers. The WebKit approach uses pseudo-elements with separate track and thumb styling, while Firefox uses a simpler two-property shorthand. This generator outputs both formats simultaneously.

faq.q: Which browsers support custom scrollbars?
faq.a: WebKit-based browsers (Chrome, Edge, Safari) support the -webkit-scrollbar pseudo-elements. Firefox supports scrollbar-width and scrollbar-color properties. IE does not support custom scrollbars.

faq.q: Can I make scrollbars thinner?
faq.a: Yes. Change the width value in -webkit-scrollbar and the scrollbar-width property. Note that scrollbar-width only supports auto, thin, or none — not custom pixel values.

faq.q: Do custom scrollbars affect accessibility?
faq.a: Thin or invisible scrollbars can make content difficult to navigate for users who rely on visible scroll indicators. Keep scrollbars visible and reasonably sized for accessibility.

whatIs: The Responsive Breakpoint Tester lets you preview content at specific viewport widths without resizing your browser window. It provides preset buttons for common device widths — iPhone SE (375px), iPad (768px), Laptop (1024px), Desktop (1280px), and Wide (1536px) — and renders a preview container at the selected width to verify how your CSS breakpoints respond.
howToUse: Click one of the preset device buttons to set the preview width.
The preview container resizes to the selected width, showing how content would appear at that viewport size.
Set your CSS breakpoints in your own stylesheet and observe how the preview container responds at different widths.
whyUse: Testing responsive layouts requires viewing content at multiple viewport widths. While browser dev tools provide responsive mode, this tool offers quick one-click switching between common device widths without opening developer tools. It is useful for rapid breakpoint verification during CSS development.

faq.q: Does this simulate actual device rendering?
faq.a: No. This tool adjusts the container width but does not change the browser's viewport, device pixel ratio, or user agent. Use browser dev tools for accurate device simulation.

faq.q: What widths should I test?
faq.a: The presets cover the most common breakpoints: mobile (375), tablet (768), laptop (1024), desktop (1280), and wide (1536). Match these to your project's CSS breakpoints.

faq.q: Can I test custom widths?
faq.a: The current presets are fixed. For custom widths, use your browser's responsive dev tools for more flexible testing.

whatIs: The Viewport Size Simulator displays the current browser viewport dimensions, device pixel ratio (DPR), and common CSS breakpoint thresholds. It reports the actual window width and height, the DPR value for understanding retina displays, and lists the standard Tailwind CSS breakpoints (sm: 640px through 2xl: 1536px) for quick reference.
howToUse: Click the Transform button to display current viewport information.
The output shows the viewport width, height, and device pixel ratio.
A reference list of common breakpoints is included for comparison against your current viewport size.
whyUse: Understanding your current viewport size is essential when writing responsive CSS. The DPR value reveals whether you are testing on a retina display, which affects how CSS pixels map to physical pixels. The breakpoint reference helps you immediately see which Tailwind or Bootstrap breakpoints your current viewport falls within.

faq.q: What is device pixel ratio?
faq.a: DPR is the ratio between physical pixels and CSS pixels. A DPR of 2 means each CSS pixel maps to a 2x2 grid of physical pixels (retina display). DPR of 3 is common on mobile devices.

faq.q: Why do the breakpoint values matter?
faq.a: Breakpoints define where your CSS media queries trigger. Knowing your current viewport width against these values tells you which responsive styles are currently active.

faq.q: Does this update automatically?
faq.a: The viewport information is captured at the moment you click Transform. Resize your browser and click again to get updated values.
